passage:
Sarika had skipped three Sundays at her mother's flat in Salt Lake. Work, she told herself. The truth was simpler: every visit, Amma looked smaller.

This Sunday she went. Lavanya was at the window, a shawl over her shoulders in April, and when she poured the tea her hand trembled so much the cup rattled on the saucer. Sarika's chest went tight. What if something happened and she didn't know what to do? What if she was not enough?

She took the pot gently. "Let me." Then, instead of checking her phone, she sat on the floor by Amma's chair. "Amma, is there anything you want to do this year? Anything at all?"

Lavanya was quiet, surprised. "I'd like to see the Durga pujo at my old para once more. And I want my books to go to the school library."

Sarika wrote both down. She stayed until dark and came back on Wednesday.

qa.q: How many Sundays had Sarika skipped?
qa.a: Sarika had skipped three Sundays.

qa.q: What was Sarika afraid of when she saw her mother's hand tremble?
qa.a: Sarika felt a tight fear of losing her mother and of not being enough if something happened.

qa.q: What did Sarika do that eased the fear into action?
qa.a: She stayed and sat close, asked her mother what she wanted this year, wrote down the answers and came back on Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt when Sarika asked about her wishes?
qa.a: Lavanya was surprised and probably glad to be asked, since she answered with two clear wishes.

grounding: The passage shows someone who fears losing a frail parent and has been avoiding visits, then chooses to spend real time and ask about the parent's wishes.

passage:
"You're here for twenty minutes again?" Pallavi said, arms folded in the hallway. "Aai fell last week, Uday."

"I know. I know." Uday stared at the shoe rack. "Every time I come, she's thinner. I sit there and I don't know what to say. I can't fix any of it."

"Nobody's asking you to fix it."

"I'm scared, Pallu. Of the phone ringing at night. Of being useless when it does."

Pallavi's face softened. "So am I. That's why I need you here, not in the car with the engine running."

From the bedroom, their mother called, "Are you two fighting?"

Uday went in and sat on the bed. "Aai, can I ask you something? After the fall, do you want to stay in this flat, or come to us?"

She looked at him for a long moment. "Nobody asked me that yet. I want to stay. With a bell by the bed."

"Then we'll get a bell," Uday said, and stayed for dinner.

qa.q: What did Aai want after her fall?
qa.a: She wanted to stay in the flat, with a bell by the bed.

qa.q: What was Uday afraid of?
qa.a: Uday was scared of the phone ringing at night and of being useless when it did.

qa.q: Why was asking his mother about her wishes a good step for Uday?
qa.a: It gave him something real to do with his fear, turned a short visit into real time together, and respected her choice.

qa.q: How does Pallavi see Uday's short visits?
qa.a: Pallavi feels frustrated and left alone with it at first, then understanding once she hears he is scared too.

grounding: A dialogue shows a young man afraid of losing his frail mother who has been keeping visits short, then staying and asking about her wishes.

passage:
Nazia, when you asked me on the show what caring for my mother is like, I said "fine". I'm Manoj, her son, and it wasn't fine. Let me say it properly.

Amma has had kidney trouble for two years. Every Tuesday and Friday I take her to dialysis. I sit in that hospital corridor four hours, working on my laptop, then drive her home. I love her. And some Tuesdays, stuck in traffic, I felt like the walls were closing in.

My sister Radhika lives an hour away. I never asked her for anything, because it felt like admitting I was failing Amma.

In January I finally called. "Radhika, I can't do both days. Can you take Fridays?" There was silence, then, "Why didn't you say so a year ago?" Now she does Fridays and I do Tuesdays.

Asking for help wasn't betraying Amma. It's what's letting me keep going.

qa.q: On which days does Manoj take his mother to dialysis?
qa.a: He takes her every Tuesday and Friday.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling on some Tuesdays in traffic?
qa.a: Manoj felt trapped, like the walls were closing in, even though he loved his mother.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that made the care more manageable?
qa.a: He asked his sister for one specific thing, taking Fridays, instead of carrying it all alone out of a sense of duty.

qa.q: How did Radhika seem to feel when Manoj finally asked?
qa.a: Radhika seemed surprised and a little hurt that he hadn't asked a year earlier, and willing to help.

grounding: A spoken account shows a young man whose parent leans on him for medical trips, feeling love and being trapped, who shares the load with a sibling.

passage:
Monday. Papa called Vandana at 5:10, 5:40 and 6:15. "When are you coming? The house is too quiet." Since Mummy died, he wanted her there every evening. Vandana cancelled her pottery class for the fourth week and sat with him through the news, loving him and feeling the walls press in.

Thursday. On the bus she called her sister in Pune. "Reena, I need you to do something specific. Video-call Papa every evening at seven. Every single one." Reena hesitated. "I didn't know he was calling you so much." "He is. And I'm not managing." Reena agreed, and said she'd come for two weekends a month.

Three weeks later. On Tuesday evening Vandana's hands were grey with clay. At seven, Papa was laughing at something Reena said on the tablet, and Sharma uncle from next door had come for carrom. Vandana still visited four evenings a week, but now she wanted to.

qa.a: He called her three times, at 5:10, 5:40 and 6:15.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel sitting with Papa on Monday?

qa.q: How might Reena feel after learning how often Papa called Vandana?

passage:
I found the tablets in the money plant pot. Eleven of them, white, half-melted in the soil. Appa had been "taking" his blood pressure pills for two weeks.

My first instinct was to march in with the pot. I'm Kavitha, the daughter in the family who argues; Tarun always says I could win a debate with a wall. But I had argued every morning that month, and every morning Appa got more stubborn.

So I sat down and asked what he disliked about them. "They make me go to the bathroom all night. I'm not a child to be watched."

That was new. I said, "Would you rather take them with breakfast or with lunch? Or should we ask Dr. Nair if there's another way?"

He chose lunch, grudgingly. At the next appointment, I let Dr. Nair explain things while I stayed quiet. Appa listened to her. He still grumbles, but the pot has only soil in it now.

qa.q: How many tablets did Kavitha find in the money plant pot?
qa.a: Eleven tablets were found in the money plant pot.

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling when she found the tablets?
qa.a: Kavitha felt frustrated and worried, and her first urge was to march in and argue.

qa.q: Why did offering choices work better than arguing?
qa.a: Asking why and giving Appa choices protected his dignity, and letting the doctor explain took the daily fight out of it.

qa.q: How does Appa see being watched over his medicines?
qa.a: Appa feels treated like a child and resents losing control, which is why he said he was "not a child to be watched".

grounding: A first-person account shows an adult child frustrated and worried by an ageing parent who skips medicines, who offers choices and involves the doctor instead of fighting.

passage:
Home physiotherapy note, week three. Client: Lokesh, 71, recovering from a hip operation. Family member present: his son Vijay, 25.

Lokesh again refused the walker today. "I've walked since before you were born." Vijay's jaw was tight; he told me quietly in the kitchen that they have fought about it every morning, and that he lies awake afraid his father will fall on the stairs.

During the session Vijay kept saying "Papa, use it" in a raised voice, and each time Lokesh gripped the railing harder.

I suggested Vijay step back and let me offer options instead. I asked Lokesh whether he would prefer the walker only for the stairs, or a stick for the whole house. He chose the walker for the stairs.

Next step: I have asked Vijay to invite Lokesh's old friend from the post office, whom he respects, for tea on Friday. I'll return Monday.

qa.q: What operation was Lokesh recovering from?
qa.a: Lokesh was recovering from a hip operation.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling about his father refusing the walker?
qa.a: Vijay felt frustrated and anxious, his jaw tight, lying awake afraid his father would fall on the stairs.

qa.q: What did the physiotherapist suggest instead of daily arguing?
qa.a: Offering Lokesh choices, such as the walker only for stairs, and bringing in an old friend he respects.

qa.q: How might Lokesh experience Vijay's raised voice?

grounding: A physiotherapist's note shows a young man frustrated and worried by his proud father refusing help, and shows choices and a trusted person taking the place of daily fights.

passage:
Parveen, you think you are the first child to live far from her parents? Sit. Your Samir chacha has a story.

At twenty-four I got a job in Muscat. Ammi and Abbu stayed in Lucknow. The first year, I sent money and felt guilty every day. Every festival photo from home was a knife. I would lie awake calculating how old Abbu was, and do nothing except feel terrible.

Then Ammi fell in the courtyard and a neighbour found her. That woke me up. Guilt that only hurts is useless, beta. So I changed things. I called every Sunday at nine, same time, so they could wait for it. I paid a boy from the lane to bring vegetables and check on them daily. I came home every Eid, and when I came, I switched off my phone.

I still missed them. But I stopped drowning in it and started doing something.

qa.q: Where did young Samir work, and where did his parents live?
qa.a: He worked in Muscat, and his parents stayed in Lucknow.

qa.q: How did young Samir feel during his first year away?
qa.a: He felt guilty every day, lying awake and feeling terrible without doing anything about it.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Samir's story?
qa.a: His mother's fall in the courtyard made him turn guilt into action: regular Sunday calls, a boy to check on them daily, and full attention on Eid visits.

qa.q: How might Ammi and Abbu have felt once the Sunday calls began?
qa.a: They probably felt comforted and looked forward to the fixed time, knowing their son would call.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young man living far from his parents for work, whose guilt first torments him and then moves him to regular contact, practical support and real visits.

passage:
The rain had cut the railway line to Siliguri, and Sudha's leave application had been rejected that morning. In her Bengaluru PG, she watched her mother on a video call trying to stand up from the sofa after the fall. It took three tries.

"Don't come, Sudha, the trains aren't even running," Ma said. Sudha felt sick with guilt. Everyone else's daughter lived nearby.

She let herself cry for ten minutes. Then she opened a notebook. She called Shreya, the neighbours' daughter, who worked from home. "Could you look in on Ma each evening? I'll pay for anything she needs." Shreya said yes at once. Sudha ordered groceries to be delivered, set a daily nine o'clock video call, and spoke to her manager about working from Siliguri for two weeks next month.

That night Ma said, "You're far, but you're here." Sudha slept, for the first time in two days.

qa.q: What had cut the railway line to Siliguri?
qa.a: The rain had cut the railway line.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling as she watched her mother try to stand?
qa.a: Sudha felt sick with guilt at being far away while her mother struggled.

qa.q: How did Sudha use her guilt well?

qa.q: What is it like for Sudha's mother after the plan is in place?

grounding: The story shows a young woman living far from her parent for work, whose guilt moves her to arrange practical support, regular contact and an honest visit.

passage:
Daniel had driven to his mother's house in Stockport every evening for eight months. He sorted her tablets into the weekly box, fixed the boiler, sat through the same quiz show. His sister Ada lived forty minutes away and came at Christmas.

One Thursday Ada texted: "How's Mum? Busy week here!" Daniel read it in the car park and felt something hot and sour rise in his throat. Used. That was the word.

He typed a long, angry reply, then deleted it. Instead he wrote: "She's okay. I need two things from you. Take the first Saturday of every month, the whole day. And do her online shopping order each Sunday."

Three dots, for a long time. Then: "I can do the shopping. Saturdays are hard."

Daniel breathed out. He accepted the shopping, then rang the council about a carer visiting twice a week. If Ada stayed away on Saturdays, he wouldn't stay alone.

qa.q: How long had Daniel been driving to his mother's house every evening?
qa.a: He had been driving there every evening for eight months.

qa.q: What did Daniel feel when he read Ada's text in the car park?
qa.a: Daniel felt used and bitter, something hot and sour rising in his throat.

qa.q: Why was Daniel's second message better than the angry one?
qa.a: It asked Ada for specific tasks she could say yes or no to, instead of a vague sense of duty, and he found outside help for the gap.

qa.q: How might Ada see Daniel's clear request?
qa.a: Ada may feel caught out and a bit guilty, taking the time to reply and agreeing to the shopping while pushing back on Saturdays.

grounding: The passage shows a man doing most of the caregiving while his sibling does little, who feels used and bitter, asks for specific tasks and accepts outside help.

passage:
The clinic waiting room at the geriatric OPD smelled of phenyl, and Ira had been there since eight. Her father dozed in the wheelchair beside her. This was the sixth appointment she had taken leave for this year. Chandrika had managed none.

Her phone buzzed. Chandrika: "Sorry di, the office is crazy. Tell Papa hi."

Ira's face went hot. She wanted to throw the phone across the room. Instead she waited until the tightness in her chest eased, then typed: "I can't do all of them. Please take the April and May appointments. The dates are the 9th and the 21st."

The social worker at the desk, noticing her, came over. "There is a day-care programme here for elders, three days a week. It could give you some breathing room." Ira took the form.

When her name was called, Chandrika had replied: "April 9 okay. May, I'll try." Ira filled in the day-care form anyway.

qa.q: How many appointments had Ira taken leave for that year?
qa.a: It was the sixth appointment she had taken leave for.

qa.q: How did Ira feel when Chandrika's text arrived?
qa.a: Ira felt angry and bitter, her face hot, wanting to throw the phone.

qa.q: How did Ira handle her resentment wisely?
qa.a: She waited to calm down, asked Chandrika for specific dates, and also applied for the day-care programme in case her sister stayed absent.

qa.q: How does Chandrika seem to see the caregiving?
qa.a: Chandrika seems to see it as something she can send greetings to, until Ira's specific request pushes her to commit to one date.

grounding: The passage shows a young woman doing most of the care for her father while her sister does little, who asks for specific help and accepts outside support.

In Pranav's village near Dharwad, the power went off every afternoon, so he fanned his mother by hand while she napped. Since her stroke she could barely lift a spoon.

Sometimes, fanning her, he remembered the year of his board exams. She had walked four kilometres to the bus stand every morning with him, carrying his tiffin, and waited at the gate until he came out. He hadn't thanked her then. He was sixteen and embarrassed.

Now he combed her hair slowly, the way she used to comb his. When she spilled her tea, he wiped it and said, "No hurry, Avva."

His friend Tanvir came by one evening and found him asleep sitting up. "You look worse than her," he said. "Go and lie down. I'll sit with Avva. And show that back of yours at the health centre tomorrow."

Pranav slept three hours straight. The next morning he went to the health centre.

qa.q: How far did Pranav's mother walk with him each morning during his board exams?
qa.a: She walked four kilometres to the bus stand with him.

qa.q: What does Pranav's slow combing of his mother's hair suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests deep gratitude and tenderness, remembering all she did for him when he was young.

qa.q: What did Tanvir help Pranav see?
qa.a: That caring for Avva also means resting and seeing to his own health, so he can keep going.

qa.q: How does Tanvir see Pranav's situation?
qa.a: Tanvir is worried about his friend, noticing he looks worn out, and steps in so Pranav can rest.

passage:
Sumit, you think your father is the first one to call a son home? Listen to your Jatin tauji.

When I was twenty-six, I had a good job in Delhi and a girl I wanted to marry. Then my father's eyes began to fail. He phoned and said, "A son's first duty is his father. Leave Delhi. Come back to Meerut." My mother cried in the background.

I felt pulled in half. I loved him. And I knew if I gave up everything I would resent him for the rest of his life.

So I went home one weekend and said it plainly. "Papa, I can't leave my job. But I can come every Saturday, I'll find someone to read to you in the afternoons, and I'll ask for a transfer to Ghaziabad." He sulked for a month. The transfer came the next spring. I married in December. He danced at my wedding.

qa.q: What did Jatin's father ask him to do when his eyes began to fail?
qa.a: He asked Jatin to leave Delhi and come back to Meerut.

qa.q: How did young Jatin feel when his father called?
qa.a: He felt pulled in half, loving his father but afraid he would resent him if he gave up everything.

qa.q: What choice in the story honoured both the father and Jatin's own life?
qa.a: Going home to speak plainly and offering weekly visits, a reader for the afternoons and a transfer closer, instead of quitting his job.

qa.q: How might Jatin's father have felt during the month he sulked?
qa.a: He was likely hurt and disappointed that his son did not simply obey, though he later came round and danced at the wedding.

grounding: An elder's story shows a young man whose parent calls it his duty to give up his job, feeling love and pressure, who finds an arrangement that honours both and speaks honestly.

passage:
The offer letter from the Singapore office gave Zubin forty-eight hours to sign. He read it in the hospital canteen, where his mother was recovering from a knee replacement upstairs.

When he told her, she turned to the wall. "Your father left me alone for work. Now you. A son stays." The nurse came in to take her pressure and Zubin went out to the corridor, heart pounding. He loved her. He also wanted this job more than anything in years.

He spent the night making calls. His cousin Freny could move into the spare room. A day attendant could come from eight to six. He called the office and asked if the start could move by two months.

In the morning he sat by her bed. "Mamma, I'm going, but not yet, and not leaving you alone. I'll be here until you can walk to the market. Then I'll call daily and come every three months."

She didn't answer. But she held his hand.

qa.q: How long did the offer letter give Zubin to sign?
qa.a: It gave him forty-eight hours.

qa.a: Zubin felt torn and anxious, his heart pounding, loving her but wanting the job badly.

qa.q: What might Zubin's mother be feeling when she holds his hand?

grounding: The story shows a young man whose parent calls it his duty to give up a job abroad, feeling love and pressure, who finds an arrangement that honours both lives and speaks honestly about limits.

passage:
The monsoon had knocked out the lift again, and Yash had a project deadline at midnight. His mother Irawati sat at the dining table with her tea going cold.

"Yash, is it Tuesday today?"

"Yes, Ma." Ten minutes later: "Is it Tuesday?" By the sixth time he snapped. "Ma! I told you! It's Tuesday!"

She flinched like a child. Then she said very quietly, "I'm sorry. I forget things now."

Yash shut the laptop. The shame came so fast it hurt more than the irritation had. He knelt by her chair. "No, I'm sorry. It's not your fault."

That week he booked the memory clinic the neurologist had mentioned, and read their leaflet twice. He wrote the day and date on a whiteboard by her chair. He called his Mausi and asked her to come Thursdays. And when Ma asked again, he just pointed at the board and smiled.

qa.q: What did Yash write on the whiteboard?
qa.a: He wrote the day and date on a whiteboard by her chair.

qa.q: What did Yash feel after he snapped at his mother?
qa.a: Yash felt a rush of shame, stronger than the irritation he had felt before.

qa.q: How did Yash turn his helplessness into useful steps?
qa.a: He apologised, booked the memory clinic and read their leaflet, set up a whiteboard, and asked his Mausi to share Thursdays.

qa.q: What is it like for Irawati when Yash snaps at her?
qa.a: Irawati feels frightened and ashamed, flinching and apologising for forgetting.

grounding: The story shows a young man watching his mother's memory fade, feeling helpless and irritated, then ashamed, and getting information, sharing the load and treating her with patience.

passage:
In the Andheri flat, the steel tumbler hit the floor for the third time that morning. Hemant's father looked at his right hand as if it belonged to someone else. Since the stroke in February, the hand simply stopped listening.

"Papa, carefully!" Hemant said, louder than he meant. Then he stood in the kitchen with the cloth, cheeks burning. He wasn't angry at Papa. He was angry that he could do nothing.

That evening his brother Varun came over from Thane. Hemant admitted it in the stairwell. "I shouted at him over a glass. I feel like a monster."

"I did the same last week," Varun said. "We're tired. Let's split it. I'll take weekends."

Hemant asked the physiotherapist for hand exercises and bought a plastic tumbler with two handles. Next morning Papa lifted it and drank without spilling. Hemant clapped, and Papa laughed for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: When did Hemant's father have the stroke?
qa.a: He had the stroke in February.

qa.q: Why did Hemant feel like a monster?
qa.a: Hemant felt ashamed after shouting at Papa, knowing his anger really came from feeling helpless.

qa.q: What steps helped Hemant cope?

grounding: The passage shows a young man watching his father lose strength, helpless and irritated then ashamed, who shares the load, gets information and treats him with patience.

passage:
I'm Harish, and for thirty years I was "the one who isn't Alka". Alka topped the class. Alka got the scholarship. At every wedding, some aunt would ask me what I was doing now, in a voice that already knew.

So when Appa died and the house in Mysuru had to be divided, I was ready for battle. I had lists. I had old grudges. I rehearsed what I'd say about who paid for Appa's hospital stays.

Then Alka arrived at the house with a box of old photos. There was one of the two of us on the scooter, me on the front, her arms around me so I wouldn't fall.

I put my lists away. At dinner I said, "I've felt compared with you my whole life, and I don't want this house to be one more contest. Can we just say fairly what each of us wants?" Alka's eyes filled. "I felt compared too," she said.

qa.q: What did Alka bring to the house?
qa.a: She brought a box of old photos.

qa.q: How did Harish feel as he prepared for the house discussion?
qa.a: Harish felt bitter and ready for battle, carrying decades of hurt from being compared with Alka.

qa.q: What changed the way Harish handled the house?
qa.a: Remembering the bond in the photo led Harish to put away the score-keeping and ask to talk fairly and openly.

qa.q: How might Alka have experienced the years of comparison?
qa.a: Alka seems to have felt the pressure too, as her tears and reply show she was also hurt by being compared.

grounding: A first-person account shows a sibling long compared with their sister, now tempted to compete over the family house, who remembers the bond and speaks fairly and openly.

passage:
Family counselling note, second session with sisters Devika (26) and Lavanya (29), at their request.

The topic was their late grandmother's gold bangles, which their mother wants to divide this Diwali. Devika spoke first and fast. "Lavanya always got the good things. Her dance class, her wedding sari. I'm not letting it happen again." She kept a tally on her fingers as she spoke. Lavanya sat back, arms crossed, and said little.

I asked Devika what the bangles meant to her. She stopped. "Nani used to jingle them to wake me up." Her voice cracked. For a moment the tally stopped.

I asked each of them to name one memory of the other that they were grateful for. Lavanya named Devika nursing her through typhoid. Devika laughed, surprised, and wiped her eyes.

Plan: before the next session, each will write down what she wants and why, plainly. Their mother will read both.

qa.q: What were the sisters discussing in the session?
qa.a: They were discussing their late grandmother's gold bangles.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling when she kept a tally on her fingers?
qa.a: Devika felt resentful and competitive, afraid of losing out again as she felt she always had.

qa.q: How did the counsellor move the sisters away from score-keeping?
qa.a: By asking what the bangles meant and asking each to share a grateful memory of the other, before planning a plain, fair statement of wants.

qa.q: How might Lavanya have felt hearing Devika's list?
qa.a: Lavanya probably felt accused and defensive, sitting back with arms crossed.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a young woman who felt compared with her sister and now competes over family property, and a turn toward the bond and fair, open talk.

passage:
Asif, beta, you're worried your brother is jealous of you. Let your Varun uncle tell you about mine.

When I was twenty-five, my younger brother Sunil told me at our cousin's wedding, "You got everything. Engineering college, Papa's scooter, the flat in Pune. I got the leftovers." He was drunk and shouting. People stared.

My first answer was ready in my mouth: I studied harder, I earned the flat. I swallowed it. I felt guilty, and honestly confused. I thought I had simply been lucky.

Next day I went to his room. I said, "Tell me all of it. I won't argue." He talked for an hour. Some of it was true. Papa did pay my fees and not his. I told him, "That was unfair to you. I'm sorry."

But when he said I should give him my flat, I said no. We managed to stay brothers anyway.

qa.q: What did Sunil say Varun got that he did not?
qa.a: He said Varun got engineering college, Papa's scooter and the flat in Pune.

qa.q: How did young Varun feel when Sunil shouted at the wedding?

qa.q: What was the turning point in Varun's story?

The caterers were late, forty guests were arriving for Papa's sixtieth birthday in an hour, and Anupam chose that moment, in the kitchen, to say it. "Of course Mridul gets to give the speech. Mridul got the study abroad, Mridul gets the praise. I stayed here and ran the shop."

Mridul's hands froze on the samosa tray. His first thought was, I earned that scholarship. His second was quieter: had he ever once thanked Anupam for staying?

He put the tray down. "Say the rest. I'm listening."

Anupam did, in a rush. Mridul didn't argue. "You're right that you carried the shop and nobody said so. That wasn't fair. I'm sorry."

Anupam wiped his face. "So you'll stay in India now?"

"No. My job is in Toronto, and I need it. But the speech is yours tonight, and I'll say thank you in it too." The doorbell rang. They carried the trays out together.

qa.q: How many guests were arriving for Papa's birthday?
qa.a: Forty guests were arriving.

qa.q: What was Mridul feeling when Anupam spoke in the kitchen?
qa.a: Mridul felt a flash of defensiveness and then guilt, wondering if he had ever thanked Anupam for staying.

qa.q: What did Mridul get right in the kitchen?
qa.a: He listened without defending, acknowledged the unfairness, and still kept his job in Toronto instead of buying peace with it.

qa.q: How does Anupam see the family's praise for Mridul?
qa.a: Anupam feels overlooked and resentful, as if his years running the shop were invisible.

grounding: The story shows a young man whose sibling resents him for being favoured, who listens without defending, acknowledges what was unfair, and keeps what he honestly needs.
